The Electoral College. The system by which Americans indirectly elect the president through state-based electors rather than through a direct popular vote, the Electoral College was established by the Constitution in 1787 as a compromise between small and large states. It distributes electoral power according to representation in Congress and has produced periodic crises, making it one of American democracy's most debated institutions.

Each state receives a number of electors equal to its total representation in Congress: Senate seats plus House seats, currently totaling 538. To win the presidency, a candidate must secure an absolute majority of 270 electoral votes out of 538. In most states, electors are bound by law or party loyalty to vote for the candidate who won the popular vote in that state under the winner-take-all system.

The Electoral College emerged from the Constitutional Convention's compromise between states seeking direct popular election and those wanting to protect state power. Critics argue that it gives disproportionate power to small states and swing states while rendering voter preference in safe states irrelevant. Wyoming, with only point two percent of the population, has roughly one point eight percent of electoral votes, while California's electoral power per capita is reduced by the winner-take-all system.

The Election of 1824 produced a constitutional crisis when no candidate won an electoral majority, and the House decided the election, sparking charges of corruption. The Election of 2000 saw George W. Bush win the presidency despite losing the national popular vote, reigniting demands for electoral reform. The "faithless elector" problem—electors voting contrary to state results or their pledges—has recurred sporadically but rarely changed outcomes due to the College's structural inefficiency. Proposed reforms range from abolishing the Electoral College entirely, requiring a constitutional amendment, to adopting the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would allocate votes to the national popular winner without amending the Constitution.
